title: The hovercraft and the coffee tin
hook: The hovercraft was proved in a kitchen with two tins, a blower and some scales.
peek: In 1955, the engineer Christopher Cockerell put an empty cat-food tin inside a coffee tin, blew air between them, and weighed the push on a pair of kitchen scales. That simple test showed a craft could float on a cushion of air.
lede: Christopher Cockerell was a radio engineer who had moved on to running a boat-hire business on the Norfolk Broads. He wanted boats to go faster by lifting them off the water. In 1955 he tested his idea with what was to hand: a cat-food tin, a coffee tin, an air blower and kitchen scales.

bullets.text: Cockerell placed the smaller tin inside the larger one, with a gap between them, and blew air down into it. The air rushed out through the narrow ring around the edge. Pointed down at a set of scales, it pushed much harder than air blown from a single open tin.

The ring of fast air acted like a curtain, trapping a cushion of higher-pressure air underneath. The craft did not need a tight seal to the ground. It could ride on air while hardly touching the surface below.
Cockerell patented the idea in 1955. The British government briefly treated it as secret, as a possible military invention, before deciding it was mainly for civilian use and backing its development.
On 25 July 1959 the SR.N1 hovercraft crossed the English Channel, 50 years to the day after Louis Blériot first flew across it. Cockerell was knighted in 1969.
